thread_title: S. flava var. atropurpurea 2AT 'super dark' Okaloosa Co, FL
breadcrumb: S. flava var. atropurpurea 2AT 'super dark' Okaloosa Co, FL

posts.body_html:
This thing can get almost solid black from head to toe, hopefully the traps will darken up even more this year as they age. It was way darker two years ago, but I didn't get any pics of it unfortuately (they're hard for amateurs like myself to photograph). So what's so special about this clone? While it is painfully slow growing, it colors up very easily like Waccamaw, but unlike waccamaw, this plant gets way darker: the traps start off all red under optimal conditions, and to date, this clone is the darkest atropurpurea in the collection. Quality-wise, I predict this is probably the second most valuable plant I have in the collection. Maybe my son Benny has a plant that I can name after him, although thing is, he's indoors all the time, so he's really white...not sure the plant fits him....maybe he'll tan well as he gets older, we'll see LOL

Thing is, what you're seeing is the very beginning of black flava breeding. in 10-20 years, this clone might be forgotten because of what potentially can be unlocked using these genetics in breeding! Yes, I have preliminary results that haven't been publicly disclosed, those stories will be shared in the future..

Anyways, that dark, almost black coloration (which, BTW, is not yet captured in the pics below) is what makes this plant stand out from the rest, along with the ease by which it colors up. The chances of finding something like this in a seed batch is incredibly low, I grew out hundreds upon hundreds of plants to find this one individual! Also, you can't just select atropurpureas as smaller seedlings with adult pitchers, you really have to grow them almost all the way out to find out which ones are the winners. I had several other candidates show very dark to almost black pitchers under lights, but as they were grown outdoors, they weren't special like this clone. As a heads up, because this clone is so slow growing, I don't want to make promises about distributing it anytime soon, but it's good for everyone to know that something like this exists and it's being worked on for future distribution.

S. flava var. atropurpurea 2AT 'super dark' Okaloosa Co, FL, photos taken a few days ago. yeah, I probably should have called it S. flava var. atropurpurea 'BLACK' but there's too many labels to change:


Traps start out red, but under optimal conditions, they slowly turn almost black as they age:




Love the dipped(ish) lip on this clone:

When my wife and I were first dating, I took her to California Carnivores and she met Peter D'Amato for the very first time. She and Peter were talking about relationships, and the topic of cheaters came up: my wife was suspicious of me at first because I'd come home at late night hours, or have to abruptly end a date because I have to "go home and water." Imagine you don't have a massive Sarracenia collection and met a stranger giving you this weird alibi, sounds pretty fake, doesn't it? Fortunately, probably 90% + of you reading this know I ain't Bee Essin maaan, you've seen my crops! Anyways, Peter helped dispel the apparent mistrust by explaining to my wife that "the plants are [my] mistress!" She doesn't need to worry about me checking out girls without her knowing, but she better be worried if she sees me ordering a new plant! LOL

Perhaps not being in the plant world, having plants being your mistress might come as a shock to some. Fortunately, when my wife first met my mom (after the California Carnivores meeting), that was when my trust was finally earned: my mom vouched for me that my whole life, she saw me with a flashlight at night watering plants as I was growing up, but she didn't see me taking random girls home....ever!

The way I look at this clone makes my wife jealous: she still comes up to me and jokingly interrogates me about a possible second family that I've started in the basement. Hey, at least you guys understand the truth, right?! I guess women can be the achille's heel for many men, but my achille's heel is S. flava var. atropurpurea 'super dark' Okaloosa Co, FL LOL!!!!

posts.body_html:
Hi MW. I may have said this before, but one of the defining visual features of these very dark flava is the 'silver' on the peristome. Whether this is visible because of the dark pigment of the leaf (ie, being common to all species but not necessarily visible) or is somehow an actual expression unique to the purple plants, I don't know. I suspect the former. The silver also is apparent on the ribs of the tubes in these plants, as can be seen in your pics, especially the third photo of your original post. In person, the ribs often appear a very stimulating blueish colour. But, interestingly, if touched, its lost.

You are correct to say how lucky to get one from a seed batch. I too was lucky back in 2000 to have this plant come out of Sumatra, Liberty Co wild seed. All the other seedlings were typical 'rubricorpora'. To end up with one of what are not common fully infused clones in the population is one of my true pieces of good fortune. And, a treasure at that. Through controlled selfing have produced many, many more true to type. See the silver sheen?

posts.body_html:
Those red flavas are fantastic! It does seem some races color up easier than many from, say, Bay Co., FL. The ones closer to Sumatra, FL are a bit more dependable.

The silver sheen is likely a thin wax and cutin layer put out by the cuticle of the leaf. A thick, waxy cuticle would be too hot and interfere with respiration, cooling. Some of these outer coatings form, microscopically, as platelets, while others are exuded as filaments or rods, giving the appearance of a glaucus "bloom". By rubbing these microscopic coverings, one can either rub them off or compress them to meld the particles into a layer, giving an almost oiled look (darker) to that region.

These waxes are typical products of the epidermis's outer cuticle, but may not be visible on light backgrounds.
